My friend says he takes this medicine, but I won't take it.
서연이 한국어를 공부한다지만 말은 하나도 못 해요.
Seoyeon says she studies Korean, but she can't speak at all.
가게 주인이 내일 문을 연다지만 아직 준비가 안 됐어요.
The shop owner says he opens tomorrow, but it's not ready yet.
사라가 요즘 일찍 일어난다지만 오늘도 회의에 늦었어요.
Sarah says she gets up early these days, but she was late for the meeting again today.
마이크가 이 근처에 산다지만 저는 한 번도 못 봤어요.
Mike says he lives near here, but I've never seen him.
동생이 숙제를 다 끝낸다지만 방에서 게임만 해요.
My sibling says he finishes all the homework, but he only plays games in his room.
cz: 지우가 매일 공원에서 ___ 저는 한 번도 못 봤어요. (달리다)
Jiu says she runs in the park every day, but I've never seen her.
엄마가 오늘 일찍 ___ 저는 기다리지 않을 거예요. (오다)
Mom says she's coming early today, but I won't wait.

fe: They say this bag is cheap, but it's expensive for me.
xk: 형용사와 있다/없다 뒤에 -다지만을 붙여요. 남이 '~하다'고 한 말을 받아들이고 뒤에 반대 내용을 말해요.
xe: Attach -다지만 to adjectives and 있다/없다. You accept what someone said is so, then give the opposite.
nk: 남의 평가와 내 생각이 다를 때 써요. 상대 의견을 존중하면서 내 생각을 말하는 느낌이에요. 평가가 틀렸다고 직접 말하는 것보다 부드러워요.
ne: Use it when someone else's opinion and yours differ. You acknowledge their view while giving yours. It's softer than saying their view is wrong.
ex: 친구가 그 영화가 재미있다지만 저는 졸렸어요.
My friend says that movie is fun, but I felt sleepy.
사람들이 이 식당이 맛있다지만 저는 별로예요.
People say this restaurant is good, but I don't think so.
선생님이 시험이 쉽다지만 저는 많이 걱정돼요.
The teacher says the test is easy, but I'm very worried.
뉴스에서 오늘 안 춥다지만 저는 추워요.
The news says it's not cold today, but I feel cold.
호텔 직원이 방이 깨끗하다지만 바닥에 물이 있어요.
The hotel staff says the room is clean, but there's water on the floor.
엄마가 집이 가깝다지만 걸어서 한 시간이 걸려요.
Mom says the house is close, but it takes an hour on foot.
cz: Dad says this road is bright, but I'm scared.
동생이 그 가방이___ 저는 너무 무거워요. (가볍다)
My sibling says that bag is light, but it's too heavy for me.

fk: 저 사람이 가수라지만 저는 한 번도 못 봤어요.
fe: They say that person is a singer, but I've never even seen him.
xk: 명사 뒤에 붙여서 'N(이)라고 하지만'의 뜻을 나타내요. 받침이 있으면 -이라지만, 없으면 -라지만을 써요.
xe: Attach it to a noun to mean 'although they say it is N.' Use -이라지만 after a final consonant and -라지만 after a vowel.
nk: 이름이나 직업 같은 말을 일단 받아들이고 실제는 다르다고 말할 때 써요. 의심하는 느낌이 있어요.
ne: Use it to accept a label such as a name or job for now, then say the reality differs. It carries a hint of doubt.
ex: 오늘이 휴일이라지만 저는 회사에 가야 해요.
They say today is a holiday, but I have to go to work.
They say this is a popular restaurant, but there's nobody here.
민수가 제 친구라지만 저는 그 사람을 잘 몰라요.
They say Minsu is my friend, but I don't know him well.
시험이 내일이라지만 아직 공부를 안 했어요.
They say the test is tomorrow, but I haven't studied yet.
이것이 한국 옷이라지만 평소에는 안 입어요.
They say this is Korean clothing, but I don't wear it normally.
그 사람이 사장님 아들이라지만 일을 열심히 해요.
They say he is the boss's son, but he works hard.
cz: Hajun says today is Sunday, but I have a lot of work.
Yuna says this building is a bank, but it's very small.

fk: 친구가 어제 숙제를 했다지만 저는 못 믿어요.
fe: My friend says he did the homework yesterday, but I can't believe it.
xk: 지난 일에 대한 남의 말을 받아들이고 뒤에 반대 내용을 말해요. 과거 -았/었- 뒤에 -다지만을 붙여요.
xe: You accept someone's statement about the past, then give the opposite. Add -다지만 after the past -았/었-.
nk: 그 사람의 말과 내가 본 것이 다를 때 써요. 말한 사람이 거짓말을 한다는 뜻은 아니고, 내 생각은 다르다는 거리감이 있어요.
ne: Use it when what the person said differs from what you saw. It doesn't say they're lying; it just shows you see it differently.
ex: 민수가 어제 비가 왔다지만 제 동네는 맑았어요.
Minsu says it rained yesterday, but it was sunny in my neighborhood.
서연이 그 책을 읽었다지만 내용을 몰라요.
Seoyeon says she read that book, but she doesn't know the content.
가게 주인이 어제 문을 열었다지만 문이 닫혀 있었어요.
The shop owner says he opened yesterday, but the door was closed.
동생이 방을 치웠다지만 방이 아직 더러워요.
My sibling says he cleaned the room, but it's still dirty.
사라가 어제 일찍 잤다지만 오늘도 피곤해 보여요.
Sarah says she slept early yesterday, but she looks tired today too.
They say Mike went to Korea, but there's been no word from him.
cz: Jiu says she took the medicine, but she still has a fever.
Minsu says he sent the letter, but I didn't receive it.

fe: You said it would rain, but the sky is really clear.
xk: 다른 사람이 한 말을 먼저 말하고, 뒤에는 그 말과 다른 현실을 말해요. 동사는 -ㄴ다더니/-는다더니, 형용사는 -다더니, 명사는 -(이)라더니예요.
xe: First repeat what someone said, then say the reality is different. Verbs take -ㄴ다더니/-는다더니, adjectives -다더니, nouns -(이)라더니.
nk: 들은 말이 틀렸거나 기대와 달라서 놀랐을 때 써요. 말한 사람에게 '말과 다르네'라고 불평하는 느낌도 있어요. 들은 대로여서 확인하는 때는 다른 쓰임이에요.
ne: Use it when what you heard turns out wrong or surprising. It can sound like a mild complaint: 'that's not what you said.' Confirming that what you heard is true is a different use.
ex: 민수가 매일 운동한다더니 오늘도 집에서 자고 있어요.
Minsu said he exercises every day, but he is sleeping at home again today.
They said the weather was cold, but it isn't cold at all.
이 식당이 유명하다더니 손님이 별로 없네요.
They said this restaurant is famous, but there are hardly any customers.
Seoyeon said she was a teacher, but she works at a company.
하준이 다이어트한다더니 케이크를 세 개나 먹었어요.
Hajun said he was on a diet, but he ate three cakes.
cz: Dohyun said the test was hard, but he isn't studying.
에밀리가 빵을 ___ 오늘은 빵을 맛있게 먹어요. (싫어하다)
Emily said she dislikes bread, but today she eats it happily.

fk: 지우가 이 빵집이 맛있다더니 정말 맛있네요.
fe: Jiwoo said this bakery was good, and it really is good.
xk: 다른 사람이 한 말을 먼저 말하고, 뒤에는 그 말이 맞다고 말해요. 들은 말을 내가 직접 보고 확인했을 때 써요.
xe: Repeat what someone said, then say it is true. Use it when you checked it yourself.
nk: '소문대로네'라는 느낌이에요. 뒤 문장에 '정말', '역시', '-네요'를 자주 같이 써요. 앞말과 뒤말이 다르면 반대 쓰임이 되니 문맥을 잘 봐요.
ne: It feels like 'just as they said.' It often goes with 정말, 역시 or -네요 in the second clause. If the second clause contradicts the first, it becomes the 'contrast' use, so watch the context.
ex: 지민이 요즘 바쁘다더니 오늘도 늦게까지 일하네요.
Jimin said she's busy these days, and she's working late again today.
부산 바다가 예쁘다더니 사진보다 더 예뻐요.
They said the sea in Busan is pretty, and it is prettier than the photos.
안나가 매운 음식을 잘 먹는다더니 김치찌개를 맛있게 먹어요.
Anna said she eats spicy food well, and she is enjoying the kimchi stew.
They said that place is a market, and there really are a lot of people.
서연이 노래를 잘한다더니 목소리가 정말 좋아요.
Seoyeon said she sings well, and her voice really is good.
cz: 수진이 새 식당 음식이 ___ 정말 값이 싸요. (싸다)
Sujin said the food at the new restaurant was cheap, and it really is cheap.
도현이 한국 노래를 ___ 정말 가사를 다 알아요. (좋아하다)
Dohyun said he likes Korean songs, and he really knows all the lyrics.

fk: 지금 간댔자 가게는 이미 문을 닫았어요.
fe: Even if you go now, the shop has already closed.
xk: '해도 소용없다', '해 봤자 별것 아니다'라고 말할 때 써요. 동사는 -ㄴ댔자/-는댔자, 형용사는 -댔자, 명사는 -(이)랬자예요.
xe: Use it for 'even if you do it, it's no use' or 'it's nothing much anyway.' Verbs take -ㄴ댔자/-는댔자, adjectives -댔자, nouns -(이)랬자.
nk: -아/어 봤자와 뜻이 같아요. -댔자는 '~다고 해도'의 줄임말이라 말할 때 더 자주 써요. 뒤에는 소용없다, 별것 아니다, 차이가 작다는 뜻이 와요.
ne: The meaning is the same as -아/어 봤자. -댔자 is a short form of 'even if they say/do ~', so it is more common in speech. The second part says it is useless, minor, or a small difference.
ex: Even if you run now, the train has already left.
Even if it's cheaper, it's only a few hundred won's difference.
Even if Minsu eats, it's only one bowl of ramen.
Even if she's a teacher, she's only two years older than me.
Even if I study, I can only do one hour.
cz: Even if it rains tomorrow, it will only be a little.
Even if you have a lot of money, it's no use if you aren't at peace.

fe: I slipped on the ice and fell flat on my back.
xk: 서 있던 사람이 뒤로 쿵 넘어질 때, 또는 바닥에 넘어질 때 써요. 자빠지다는 '넘어지다'보다 거친 말이에요.
xe: Use it when a standing person falls down hard, often onto their back. It is a rougher word than 넘어지다.
nk: 말할 때 쓰는 편한 말이에요. 글이나 처음 만난 사람에게는 '넘어지다'가 더 좋아요. 크게 쿵 넘어지는 모습이 떠올라요.
ne: It is casual spoken language. In writing or with people you just met, 넘어지다 is better. It suggests a big, heavy fall.
ex: 버스가 갑자기 서서 사람들이 다 자빠졌어요.
The bus stopped suddenly and everyone fell over.
The chair wobbled and Hajun fell backward.
Be careful not to fall on the snowy road.
I fell while exercising yesterday, so my knee hurts.
The baby fell while walking but didn't cry.
cz: Mike fell over while kicking the ball.
The floor is wet, so Sara keeps falling.

fe: (rude) Look at you, just goofing off instead of working.
xk: 동사 뒤에 -고 자빠지다를 붙이면 그 행동이 마음에 안 든다는 뜻이에요. 보통 -고 자빠졌네, -고 자빠졌어처럼 반말로 말해요.
xe: Adding -고 자빠지다 after a verb shows you dislike or look down on that action. It is usually said in casual speech, as -고 자빠졌네 or -고 자빠졌어.
nk: 아주 거친 말이에요. 친구 사이나 혼잣말에서 화가 났을 때 써요. 윗사람이나 처음 만난 사람에게는 쓰지 않아요.
ne: It is a very rough expression, used among friends or when talking to yourself in anger. Never use it with elders or people you just met.
ex: 숙제는 안 하고 게임만 하고 자빠졌어.
(annoyed) He isn't doing his homework, just sitting there playing games.
(annoyed) My little brother went and put on my clothes.
(rude) Look at him, sleeping at the office.
(annoyed) It's raining, so where are you going off to?
cz: 시험 공부는 안 하고 영화만 ___. (보다 + -고 자빠지다)
(annoyed) Look at him, watching movies instead of studying for the test.
가게에서 돈도 안 내고 물건을___. (가져가다 + -고 자빠지다)
(angry) The nerve! He took the goods from the shop without even paying.

fk: 일찍 일어나 버릇하면 아침이 힘들지 않아요.
fe: Once you get used to getting up early, mornings aren't hard.
xk: 같은 일을 자꾸 해서 습관이 될 때 써요. 주로 '버릇하면', '버릇해서'로 말해요.
xe: Use it when doing the same thing again and again turns it into a habit. It usually appears as 버릇하면 or 버릇해서.
nk: '그렇게 계속하면 습관이 된다'는 뜻이라 좋은 습관과 나쁜 습관에 다 써요. 지금 습관이라는 사실만 말할 때는 -곤 하다가 더 자연스러워요.
ne: It means 'if you keep doing it, it becomes a habit,' so it fits both good and bad habits. To just state a current habit, -곤 하다 sounds more natural.
ex: If you get used to eating late at night, you gain weight.
아이가 어릴 때부터 책을 읽어 버릇해서 글을 잘 써요.
The child got used to reading from a young age, so he writes well.
매일 운동해 버릇하니까 이제 안 하면 이상해요.
Since I got used to exercising every day, it feels strange when I don't.
남에게 물어 버릇해서 혼자 찾지 않아요.
I got used to asking others, so I don't look it up myself.
If you get used to taking taxis, buses feel inconvenient.
cz: I got used to drinking coffee in the morning, so I get sleepy without it.
I got used to taking notes on my phone, so paper notes are inconvenient.

fe: Jimin is asking when you're coming.
xk: 다른 사람이 한 질문을 전해요. 동사 어간에 -느냬를 붙여요. '-느냐고 해'를 줄인 말이에요.
xe: Use it to pass on a question someone else asked. Add -느냬 to a verb stem. It is short for '-느냐고 해'.
nk: 친한 사이의 반말이에요. 어른께 말하거나 글을 쓸 때는 '-느냐고 해요'를 써요. 질문한 사람의 말을 그대로 전하는 느낌이에요.
ne: This is casual speech between close people. To elders or in writing, use '-느냐고 해요'. It passes on someone's question as it was asked.
ex: Sujin is asking what you're eating today.
Hajun is asking where you live.
Mom is asking if you're done with your homework.
The store clerk is asking what you're looking for.
Seoyeon is asking where you're going this weekend.
cz: Sara is asking me what time I go to sleep.
Mike is asking when you're going to read this book.

f: A 어간+냬 / 받침 있으면 어간+으냬 또는 어간+냬
fe: Mom is asking if you're very busy today.
xk: 다른 사람이 형용사로 한 질문을 전해요. 받침이 없으면 -냬를 붙이고, 받침이 있으면 -으냬와 -냬를 둘 다 써요.
xe: Passes on a question asked with an adjective. After a vowel use -냬. After a final consonant both -으냬 and -냬 are used.
nk: 상태를 묻는 말을 전할 때 써요. 동사는 -느냬, 형용사는 -냬나 -으냬예요. 말할 때는 받침이 있어도 -냬를 많이 써요. 친구나 가족에게 하는 반말이에요.
ne: Use it to pass on a question about a state. Verbs take -느냬, adjectives take -냬 or -으냬. In speech, -냬 is common even after a final consonant. It is casual speech for friends and family.
ex: Jun is asking if you like this movie.
Minsu is asking if that bag is expensive.
Seoyeon is asking if this room is small.
Anna is asking if it's quiet there.
cz: Hajun is asking if that piece of clothing is big.
Sujin is asking if this house is spacious.

fe: Minsu is asking if you're a student.
xk: 다른 사람이 '~예요?' 하고 물은 말을 전해요. 명사 뒤에 받침이 있으면 -이냬, 없으면 -냬를 붙여요.
xe: Passes on a question like 'Is it ~?'. Add -이냬 after a final consonant and -냬 after a vowel.
nk: 사람이나 물건이 무엇인지 묻는 말을 전해요. '아니다'는 '아니냬'가 돼요. 반말이라 친한 사이에서 써요.
ne: Use it for questions about who or what something is. '아니다' becomes '아니냬'. It is casual, for close people.
ex: Jiu is asking if that person is your friend.
Mom is asking if this is your bag.
The teacher is asking who this person is.
유나가 이 책이 네 거 아니냬.
Yuna is asking if this book isn't yours.
cz: Jun is asking if that person is your younger sibling.
Anna is asking if this person is your teacher.

fe: Hajun is asking why you didn't come yesterday.
xk: 지난 일을 물은 말을 전해요. 어간에 -았/었을 붙이고 -냬를 붙여요.
xe: Passes on a question about the past. Add -았/었 to the stem, then -냬.
nk: 과거를 물을 때는 동사와 형용사 모두 -았/었냬예요. '-느냬'와 달리 -느-가 들어가지 않아요.
ne: For past questions, both verbs and adjectives take -았/었냬. Unlike -느냬, there is no -느-.
ex: Mom is asking if you ate.
Sujin is asking if you finished your homework.
Dohyun is asking if you saw that movie.
Jimin is asking where you went yesterday.
cz: Seoyeon is asking what time you got up today.
Mike is asking when the class ended.

fe: I heard the teacher asking if you're coming to school tomorrow.
xk: 내가 직접 들은 질문을 전해요. 동사 어간에 -느냐더군을 붙여요. '-느냐고 하더군'을 줄인 말이에요.
xe: Passes on a question I heard myself. Add -느냐더군 to a verb stem. It is short for '-느냐고 하더군'.
nk: '-더군'은 내가 보거나 들어서 알게 된 일을 말해요. 조금 어른스럽고 혼잣말 같은 느낌이에요. 친구에게는 '-느냐더라'를 많이 써요.
ne: '-더군' is for things I saw or heard myself. It sounds a bit mature, like talking to yourself. With friends, '-느냐더라' is more common.
ex: I heard Sujin asking where you buy that book.
I heard Anna asking what you're doing this weekend.
I heard the shop owner asking what you're looking for.
I heard Jiu asking if you exercise often.
cz: I heard Seoyeon asking when you'll watch that movie.
I heard Dohyun asking what time you get up every day.

fe: I heard Hajun asking if this bag is expensive.
xk: 내가 들은 질문을 전해요. 형용사 어간에 받침이 없으면 -냐더군, 있으면 -으냐더군을 붙여요.
xe: Passes on a question I heard. Add -냐더군 after a vowel and -으냐더군 after a final consonant.
nk: 상태를 물은 말을 전해요. 동사는 -느냐더군, 형용사는 -(으)냐더군이에요. 들은 것을 담담히 말하는 느낌이에요.
ne: Use it for a question about a state. Verbs take -느냐더군, adjectives take -(으)냐더군. It reports what I heard in a calm way.
ex: I heard the teacher asking if that room is good.
I heard Sujin asking if these shoes are small.
I heard Jiu asking if you're busy these days.
I heard Sara asking if it's quiet there.
cz: I heard Minsu asking if the things in this shop are cheap.
I heard Seoyeon asking if this room is spacious.

fe: I heard Mom asking who that person is.
xk: 내가 들은 '~예요?' 질문을 전해요. 명사 뒤에 받침이 있으면 -이냐더군, 없으면 -냐더군을 붙여요.
xe: Passes on a 'Is it ~?' question I heard. Add -이냐더군 after a final consonant and -냐더군 after a vowel.
nk: 무엇인지, 누구인지 묻는 말을 전해요. '아니다'는 '아니냐더군'이 돼요. 들은 말을 전하는 말투예요.
ne: Use it for questions about what or who something is. '아니다' becomes '아니냐더군'. It reports something I heard.
ex: I heard Anna asking if this is your bag.
I heard the teacher asking what your hobby is.
I heard Yuna asking if that person is your teacher.
I heard Mike asking what day today is.
cz: I heard Dohyun asking if this person is your older brother.
I heard Jimin asking if this is your bag.

fe: I heard Minsu asking if you ate lunch.
xk: 내가 들은 과거 질문을 전해요. 어간에 -았/었을 붙이고 -냐더군을 붙여요.
xe: Passes on a question about the past that I heard. Add -았/었 to the stem, then -냐더군.
nk: 과거를 물을 때는 동사와 형용사 모두 -았/었냐더군이에요. -느-는 들어가지 않아요.
ne: For past questions, both verbs and adjectives take -았/었냐더군. There is no -느-.
ex: I heard the teacher asking if you finished your homework.
I heard Mom asking what time you slept yesterday.
I heard Dohyun asking if you read that book.
I heard Jiu asking where you went yesterday.
cz: I heard Anna asking what you drank this morning.
I heard Seoyeon asking if you heard that news.

fe: Hajun was asking what you're doing tonight, you know.
xk: 내가 직접 들은 질문을 편하게 전해요. 동사 어간에 -느냐더라고를 붙여요. '-느냐고 하더라고'를 줄인 말이에요.
xe: Passes on a question I heard myself, in a relaxed way. Add -느냐더라고 to a verb stem. It is short for '-느냐고 하더라고'.
nk: '-더라고'는 이야기하듯 부드럽게 말해요. 친한 사이의 반말이에요. 높이려면 '-느냐더라고요'를 써요.
ne: '-더라고' sounds soft, like telling a story. It is casual speech. To be polite, add 요: '-느냐더라고요'.
ex: The clerk was asking if you're paying by card.
Mom was asking if you're coming home early today.
Sara was asking how many years you've been living in Korea.
A friend was asking if you read books every day.
cz: Yuna was asking if you often listen to that song.
Jun was asking if you're resting this weekend.

fe: Jimin was asking if that house is big, you know.
xk: 내가 들은 질문을 편하게 전해요. 형용사 어간에 받침이 없으면 -냐더라고, 있으면 -으냐더라고를 붙여요.
xe: Passes on a question I heard, casually. Add -냐더라고 after a vowel and -으냐더라고 after a final consonant.
nk: 상태를 물은 말을 전해요. 동사는 -느냐더라고, 형용사는 -(으)냐더라고예요. 친구나 가족에게 편하게 전할 때 써요.
ne: Use it for a question about a state. Verbs take -느냐더라고, adjectives take -(으)냐더라고. It fits relaxed talk.
ex: Mom was asking if that dress is pretty.
Sara was asking if there are many people there.
Dohyun was asking if that mountain is high.
Anna was asking if the shop is quiet.
cz: Sara was asking if these shoes are comfortable.
Dohyun was asking if this room is narrow.

fe: The teacher was asking what your name is, you know.
xk: 내가 들은 '~예요?' 질문을 편하게 전해요. 명사 뒤에 받침이 있으면 -이냐더라고, 없으면 -냐더라고를 붙여요.
xe: Passes on a 'Is it ~?' question I heard, casually. Add -이냐더라고 after a final consonant and -냐더라고 after a vowel.
nk: 무엇인지, 누구인지 묻는 말을 전해요. '아니다'는 '아니냐더라고'가 돼요. 친구와 이야기할 때 자주 써요.
ne: Use it for questions about what or who something is. '아니다' becomes '아니냐더라고'. It is common when chatting with friends.
ex: Emily was asking if that person is your older brother.
The shop owner was asking if this is your umbrella.
A friend was asking what day tomorrow is.
Yuna was asking if that person is your boss.
cz: Jun was asking if this is your desk.
Seoyeon was asking if that person is your neighbor.

fk: 서연이 어제 수업이 몇 시에 끝났냐더라고.
fe: Seoyeon was asking what time class ended yesterday, you know.
xk: 내가 들은 과거 질문을 편하게 전해요. 어간에 -았/었을 붙이고 -냐더라고를 붙여요.
xe: Passes on a question about the past that I heard, casually. Add -았/었 to the stem, then -냐더라고.
nk: 과거를 물을 때는 동사와 형용사 모두 -았/었냐더라고예요. -느-는 들어가지 않아요.
ne: For past questions, both verbs and adjectives take -았/었냐더라고. There is no -느-.
ex: Mom was asking if you finished your homework.
Jiu was asking if you saw that movie.
Sara was asking if you slept well yesterday.
Jun was asking where you bought your wallet.
cz: Hajun was asking if you got up early this morning.
Mike was asking if you borrowed that book.

fe: I heard the teacher asking what time you're coming tomorrow.
xk: 내가 직접 들은 질문을 정중하게 전해요. 동사 어간에 -느냐더군요를 붙여요. '-느냐고 하더군요'를 줄인 말이에요.
xe: Passes on a question I heard myself, politely. Add -느냐더군요 to a verb stem. It is short for '-느냐고 하더군요'.
nk: '-더군요'는 보거나 들어서 알게 된 일을 공손하게 말해요. 윗사람에게는 보통 -더라고요를 써요. 친구에게는 '-느냐더라'가 편해요.
ne: '-더군요' politely tells what I saw or heard. With people older than you, -더라고요 is usually the safer choice. With friends, '-느냐더라' is more relaxed.
ex: I heard a customer asking where they sell this book.
I heard Dohyun asking who you're meeting this weekend.
I heard the tour guide asking if you're taking photos.
I heard Mom asking if we're eating dinner together today.
cz: I heard a coworker asking what you're ordering for lunch.
I heard Mike asking where you live in Korea.

fe: I heard the doctor asking if it hurts a lot.
xk: 내가 들은 질문을 정중하게 전해요. 형용사 어간에 받침이 없으면 -냐더군요, 있으면 -으냐더군요를 붙여요.
xe: Passes on a question I heard, politely. Add -냐더군요 after a vowel and -으냐더군요 after a final consonant.
nk: 상태를 물은 말을 전해요. 동사는 -느냐더군요, 형용사는 -(으)냐더군요예요. 공손해서 직장이나 학교에서도 써요.
ne: Use it for a question about a state. Verbs take -느냐더군요, adjectives take -(으)냐더군요. It is polite, so it works at work or school.
ex: I heard a customer asking if this bag is big.
I heard the staff asking if this room is narrow.
I heard Yuna asking if the water is cold.
I heard Mom asking if the room is warm.
cz: I heard Seoyeon asking if this food is salty.
I heard a customer asking if this chair is low.

fe: I heard the teacher asking who this person is.
xk: 내가 들은 '~예요?' 질문을 정중하게 전해요. 명사 뒤에 받침이 있으면 -이냐더군요, 없으면 -냐더군요를 붙여요.
xe: Passes on an 'Is it ~?' question I heard, politely. Add -이냐더군요 after a final consonant and -냐더군요 after a vowel.
nk: 무엇인지, 누구인지 묻는 말을 전해요. '아니다'는 '아니냐더군요'가 돼요. 공손한 말투예요.
ne: Use it for questions about what or who something is. '아니다' becomes '아니냐더군요'. It is polite.
ex: I heard a customer asking what kind of food this is.
지우 씨가 저 건물이 네 회사냐더군요.
I heard Jiu asking if that building is your company.
I heard Sara asking what the date is today.
I heard Yuna asking if this person is your teacher.
cz: I heard the staff asking if this is the customer's umbrella.
I heard Hajun asking if that person is a neighbor.

fk: 수진 씨가 어제 몇 시에 잤냐더군요.
fe: I heard Sujin asking what time you slept yesterday.
xk: 내가 들은 과거 질문을 정중하게 전해요. 어간에 -았/었을 붙이고 -냐더군요를 붙여요.
xe: Passes on a question about the past that I heard, politely. Add -았/었 to the stem, then -냐더군요.
nk: 과거를 물을 때는 동사와 형용사 모두 -았/었냐더군요예요. -느-는 들어가지 않아요.
ne: For past questions, both verbs and adjectives take -았/었냐더군요. There is no -느-.
ex: I heard the teacher asking if you did your homework.
I heard a customer asking if you bought this book.
I heard Mom asking if you took your medicine this morning.
I heard Anna asking if you met that person.
cz: I heard Dohyun asking if you got rained on yesterday.
I heard Emily asking if you knew that news.

fe: What time does it start tomorrow, may I ask?
xk: 동사 어간에 '-는지요'를 붙여요. 정중하게 묻거나 확인할 때 써요. 'ㄹ' 받침은 빠져요(살다 → 사는지요).
xe: Add '-는지요' to a verb stem. Use it to ask or check something politely. A final 'ㄹ' drops (살다 → 사는지요).
nk: 모르는 사람, 손님, 윗사람에게 조심스럽게 물을 때 써요. '-아/어요?'보다 더 공손하고 부드러워요. 친한 친구에게는 너무 딱딱해요. 글이나 공식적인 자리에서도 자주 나와요.
ne: Use it with strangers, customers, and people above you when you want to ask carefully. It sounds softer and more polite than '-아/어요?'. It is too stiff for close friends. It also appears often in writing and formal settings.
ex: 저, 이 옷을 입어 봐도 되는지요?
Excuse me, may I try this on?
When does the meeting end, may I ask?
Do we have to hand in the homework by tomorrow?
How do I get to the airport, please?
Does this bus stop in front of City Hall?
Is my child doing well at school?
cz: Is there a pharmacy near here, may I ask?
About where is the package right now, may I ask?

fe: Are you very busy these days, may I ask?
xk: 형용사는 받침이 없으면 '-ㄴ지요', 받침이 있으면 '-은지요'를 붙여요. 명사에는 '인지요'를 붙여요. 과거는 '-았/었는지요'예요.
xe: For adjectives, add '-ㄴ지요' after a vowel and '-은지요' after a final consonant. For nouns, add '인지요'. The past is '-았/었는지요'.
nk: 상태나 정체를 정중하게 물을 때 써요. 상대가 불편하지 않게 돌려서 묻는 느낌이에요. 'ㅂ' 불규칙은 달라져요(춥다 → 추운지요). 편한 사이에서는 '-아/어요?'를 써요.
ne: Use it to ask politely about a state or an identity. It feels indirect, so the other person does not feel pushed. 'ㅂ' irregular adjectives change (춥다 → 추운지요). With close friends, use '-아/어요?' instead.
ex: Excuse me, are you perhaps Mike's friend?
Sir, is this food too spicy?
cz: Is the room too small, may I ask?
Is that person a teacher at this school, may I ask?

fe: I'm asking you, are you going to school today?
xk: 내가 한 질문에 대답이 없을 때 같은 질문을 다시 해요. 동사 어간에 '-(느)냐니까요'를 붙여요. 과거는 '-았/었냐니까요'예요.
xe: Use it to repeat your own question when you got no answer. Add '-(느)냐니까요' to a verb stem. The past is '-았/었냐니까요'.
nk: 조금 답답하거나 화난 느낌이 있어요. 가족이나 친한 친구 사이에서 써요. 윗사람에게 쓰면 무례해요. '-냐고요'는 남의 질문을 되묻지만, 이 문형은 내가 한 질문을 다시 해요.
ne: It sounds a bit impatient or annoyed. Use it with family and close friends. It is rude to people above you. '-냐고요' echoes someone else's question, but this form repeats your own question.
ex: I'm asking if you ate lunch earlier.
I'm asking where you live now.
I'm asking what this shop sells.
I'm asking what time you go to work tomorrow.
I'm asking if you gave your friend a present.
cz: 답이 없어서 다시 물어요. 어제 누구를___ (만나다).
I'm asking who you met yesterday!
답이 없어서 다시 물어요. 지갑을 어디에서 ___ (잃어버리다).
I'm asking where you lost your wallet!

fe: I'm asking you, are you really busy these days?
xk: 형용사는 받침이 없으면 '-냐니까요', 받침이 있으면 '-으냐니까요'를 붙여요. 명사는 받침이 있으면 '이냐니까요', 없으면 '냐니까요'예요.
xe: For adjectives, add '-냐니까요' after a vowel and '-으냐니까요' after a final consonant. For nouns, add '이냐니까요' after a consonant and '냐니까요' after a vowel.
nk: 상태나 정체를 물었는데 대답이 없을 때 써요. 답답한 마음이 들어가요. 과거는 '-았/었냐니까요'예요. 친한 사이에서만 쓰는 편이 좋아요.
ne: Use it when you asked about a state or an identity and got no answer. It carries some impatience. The past is '-았/었냐니까요'. It is best kept for close relationships.
ex: I'm asking how heavy these shoes are.
I'm asking if there are a lot of people in the room.
I'm asking who that person is.
I'm asking if yesterday's test was hard.
I'm asking if that person is really your friend.
cz: 답이 없어서 다시 물어요. 이 가방이 ___ (비싸다).
I'm asking if this bag is expensive!
I'm asking if that person is a doctor!

fe: What did I eat, you ask?
xk: 상대가 한 질문을 그대로 다시 말해요. 대답하기 전에 확인하거나 놀랐을 때 써요. 끝을 올려 말해요.
xe: Repeat the other person's question back to them. Use it to check before answering, or when you are surprised. Raise your voice at the end.
nk: 질문이 뜻밖이거나 잘 못 들었을 때 써요. 뒤에 바로 대답을 이어도 돼요. 말투에 따라 놀람이나 어이없음도 나타내요. '-냐니요'보다 약해서 그냥 되묻는 느낌이에요.
ne: Use it when a question is unexpected or you did not hear it well. You can follow it right away with your answer. Depending on your tone, it can also show surprise or disbelief. It is milder than '-냐니요', more of a plain echo.
ex: Whose bag is this, you ask?
What am I doing today, you ask?
Am I a student, you ask?
Did it rain a lot yesterday, you ask?
cz: A: 이 방이 조용해요? B: 방이 ___ (조용하다)? 아주 조용해요.
Is the room quiet, you ask? It's very quiet.
A: 어제 뭐 샀어요? B: 제가 어제 뭘 ___ (사다)? 모자를 샀어요.
What did I buy yesterday, you ask? I bought a hat.

fe: Mom is asking what time you're coming today.
xk: 다른 사람이 한 질문을 전해 줘요. '누가 뭐라고 했어요?'에 대답할 때 자주 써요. 누가 물었는지 앞에 말해요.
xe: Pass on a question someone else asked. It often answers 'What did they say?'. Say who asked at the start.
nk: '-냐고 해요/물어요'에서 뒤를 줄인 말이에요. 끝을 내려 말하면 전달이고, 올려 말하면 되묻기예요. 친한 사이에서 편하게 써요.
ne: It is a shortened form of '-냐고 해요/물어요'. With a falling tone it passes on a message, and with a rising tone it echoes a question. It is casual, for people you are close to.
ex: The teacher is asking if you finished all your homework.
The boss is asking if you're busy this week.
A customer is asking how much this shirt is.
Your friend is asking if you have time tomorrow.
My younger sibling is asking what time the train leaves.
cz: A: 사라 씨가 뭐라고 했어요? B: 사라가 이 길이 ___ (멀다).
Sarah is asking if this road is far.
A: 지우 씨가 뭐라고 했어요? B: 지우가 어제 어디에서 ___ (자다).
Ji-woo is asking where you slept yesterday.

fe: What do you mean, did I lie?!
xk: 상대의 질문을 되풀이하면서 놀람, 서운함, 어이없음을 나타내요. 동사 어간에 '-(느)냐니요'를 붙여요. 과거는 '-았/었냐니요'예요.
xe: Repeat the other person's question to show surprise, hurt, or disbelief. Add '-(느)냐니요' to a verb stem. The past is '-았/었냐니요'.
nk: '어떻게 그런 걸 물어요?' 하는 느낌이에요. 대답이 뻔하거나 질문이 뜻밖일 때 써요. 뒤에 '아니에요' 같은 부정이 자주 와요. '-냐고요'보다 강해서 윗사람에게는 조심해요.
ne: It feels like 'How can you ask that?'. Use it when the answer is obvious or the question is shocking. A denial such as '아니에요' often follows. It is stronger than '-냐고요', so be careful with people above you.
ex: What do you mean, did I eat breakfast?!
You're asking if I forgot our plan?!
How can you ask if I take other people's things?!
You think I'd leave on a trip without a passport?!
cz: 놀라서 말해요. 제가 어제 선생님 책을 ___ (버리다)?
You're asking if I threw away the teacher's book?!
You're asking if I fought with my friend?!

fe: You're asking if this room is small?!
xk: 형용사에는 '-냐니요'를 붙여요. 받침이 있어도 말로는 '-냐니요'를 주로 쓰고, '-으냐니요'는 딱딱하게 들려요. 명사는 받침이 있으면 '이냐니요', 없으면 '냐니요'예요. 과거는 '-았/었냐니요'예요.
xe: Add '-냐니요' to adjectives. In speech, '-냐니요' is the usual form even after a final consonant, and '-으냐니요' sounds stiff. For nouns, add '이냐니요' after a consonant and '냐니요' after a vowel. The past is '-았/었냐니요'.
nk: 상태나 정체를 묻는 말이 너무 뜻밖이라 놀랐을 때 써요. 말하는 사람은 '당연히 아니에요' 하고 생각해요. 서운하거나 화난 느낌도 들어가서 친한 사이에서 써요.
ne: Use it when a question about a state or an identity is so unexpected that it shocks you. The speaker is thinking 'Of course not'. It can also sound hurt or angry, so keep it for people you are close to.
ex: You're asking if my cooking tastes bad?!
You're asking if I'm a student?!
You're asking if this bag is fake?!
You're asking if the test was hard?!
You're asking if this job is tiring?!
cz: You're asking if this watch is cheap?! It's very expensive.
You're asking if that person is a singer?!

fe: Sujin was asking if you're coming to school tomorrow.
xk: 다른 사람이 물어본 말을 전해요. '-냐고 하던데'를 줄인 말이에요. 동사는 -느냐던데나 -냐던데를 써요.
xe: Use it to pass on a question someone else asked. It is a short form of '-냐고 하던데'. Verbs take -느냐던데 or -냐던데.
nk: 누가 이렇게 물어봤다고 가볍게 알릴 때 써요. 듣는 사람이 대답해 주면 좋겠다는 느낌이 있어요. 격식 있는 자리에서는 '-냐고 했어요'를 써요.
ne: You use it to casually report 'someone asked this.' It hints that the listener should answer. In formal settings, '-냐고 했어요' is safer.
ex: Yuna was asking what you're eating for dinner.
Our team leader was asking if you're coming to work tomorrow too.
Dohyun was asking if you've already read that book.
Seoyeon was asking where you live now.
The hotel staff was asking if you'll eat breakfast tomorrow.
cz: Mike was asking if you ate lunch.
Anna was asking what time you get up tomorrow.

fe: Hajun was asking if you're very busy these days.
xk: 형용사와 명사에 붙여서 다른 사람이 물은 말을 전해요. 받침이 있어도 말로는 -냐던데를 쓰고, -으냐던데는 딱딱하게 들려요. 명사는 N(이)냐던데를 써요.
xe: Attach it to adjectives and nouns to pass on someone else's question. In speech, -냐던데 is the usual form even after a final consonant, and -으냐던데 sounds stiff. Nouns take N(이)냐던데.
nk: 상대의 상태나 사실을 누가 궁금해했다고 알려 줄 때 써요. 동사 -느냐던데와 뜻은 같고, 붙는 말만 달라요. 말투는 가볍고 편해요.
ne: You use it when someone wondered about your state or a fact. The meaning is the same as the verb form; only what it attaches to differs. The tone is light and casual.
ex: Seoyeon was asking if that room is spacious.
The staff member was asking if that bag is new.
The teacher was asking if that movie is fun.
Mom was asking if it's cold today.
Yuna was asking if that person is your friend.
cz: Mike was asking if the food at that restaurant is good.
Jiwoo was asking if that building is a hospital.

fk: 친구가 이렇게 부탁하는데야 거절할 수 없어요.
fe: When a friend asks this way, I can't say no.
xk: 앞의 상황이 이러니 뒤의 일은 당연히 그렇다는 뜻이에요. 동사 어간에 -는데야를 붙여요. 뒤에는 '~ㄹ 수 없다', '못 V' 같은 말이 자주 와요.
xe: It means 'given this situation, the next thing naturally follows.' Add -는데야 to a verb stem. It is often followed by 'can't' or 'have to.'
nk: 앞의 상황이 너무 크거나 분명해서 다른 선택이 없다고 말할 때 써요. 그냥 이유를 말하는 -아/어서와 달리 '어쩔 수 없다'는 느낌이 강해요.
ne: You use it when the situation is so strong that there's no other choice. Unlike a plain reason with -아/어서, it strongly suggests 'there's nothing I can do.'
ex: 비가 이렇게 많이 오는데야 밖에 못 나가요.
With rain this heavy, I can't go out.
사장님이 직접 말하는데야 안 할 수 없어요.
When the boss says it in person, I have to do it.
아이가 저렇게 우는데야 그냥 갈 수 없어요.
With a child crying like that, I can't just leave.
모두 열심히 일하는데야 나도 못 쉬어요.
With everyone working hard, I can't rest either.
손님이 계속 기다리는데야 가게 문을 닫을 수 없어요.
With customers still waiting, I can't close the shop.
cz: With my sibling studying until late at night, I can't play either.
친구가 생일 파티에 ___ 안 갈 수 없어요 (초대하다).
When a friend invites me to a birthday party, I have to go.

fk: 날씨가 이렇게 추운데야 밖에 안 나가요.
fe: With weather this cold, I'm not going outside.
xk: 형용사와 명사에 붙어서 '이런 상태니 당연히 ~해요'라는 뜻이에요. 받침이 없으면 -ㄴ데야, 받침이 있으면 -은데야, 명사는 -인데야예요.
xe: With adjectives and nouns, it means 'in this state, of course ~.' Use -ㄴ데야 after a vowel, -은데야 after a final consonant, and -인데야 after a noun.
nk: 상태가 그 정도이니 다른 방법이 없다고 말할 때 써요. 동사의 -는데야와 뜻이 같아요. 뒤에는 보통 못 하거나 해야 하는 일이 와요.
ne: You use it when the state is so strong or so clear that there's no other way. The meaning is the same as verb -는데야. The ending usually says what can't or must be done.
ex: 가격이 싼데야 안 살 수 없어요.
At a price this low, I have to buy it.
With the exam tomorrow, I can't play.
방이 너무 좁은데야 친구를 부를 수 없어요.
With the room this small, I can't invite friends.
하루 종일 바쁜데야 밥도 못 먹어요.
Busy all day, I can't even eat.
집이 학교에서 먼데야 자주 못 가요.
With my home far from school, I can't go often.
cz: With water this cold, I can't swim.
오늘이 ___ 회사에 안 갈 수 없어요 (월요일).
It's Monday, so I can't skip work.

fk: 동생이 어디에 가느냐지만 말할 수 없어요.
fe: My younger sibling asks where I'm going, but I can't tell.
xk: 누가 물어본 말을 앞에 두고, 뒤에서 '하지만' 내용을 말해요. '-냐고 하지만'을 줄인 말이에요. 동사는 -느냐지만이나 -냐지만을 써요.
xe: It puts someone's question first, then gives a 'but' answer. It is a short form of '-냐고 하지만'. Verbs take -느냐지만 or -냐지만.
nk: 질문은 받았지만 대답하기 어렵거나 대답할 것이 없을 때 써요. 말하는 사람의 곤란한 마음이 들어가요. 말할 때 드물게 쓰고, 보통은 '-냐고 하지만'을 써요.
ne: You use it when you were asked but can't or won't answer. It carries the speaker's awkward feeling. It is rare in speech; '-냐고 하지만' is the usual form.
ex: 엄마가 숙제를 했냐지만 아직 시작도 못 했어요.
Mom asks if I did my homework, but I haven't even started.
회사 동료가 점심에 뭘 먹느냐지만 아직 못 정했어요.
A coworker asks what I'm eating for lunch, but I haven't decided yet.
선생님이 어제 왜 안 왔냐지만 말하기 곤란해요.
The teacher asks why I didn't come yesterday, but it's awkward to say.
여행 중에 친구가 지금 어디서 자냐지만 호텔 이름을 몰라요.
On the trip, a friend asks where I'm sleeping now, but I don't know the hotel name.
서연이 언제 이사하냐지만 날짜를 아직 몰라요.
Seoyeon asks when I'm moving, but I don't know the date yet.
cz: 사라가 저녁에 뭘___ 아직 재료가 없어요 (만들다 + -냐지만).
Sara asks what I'm making for dinner, but I don't have the ingredients yet.
도현이 어제 영화를 ___ 나는 못 봤어요 (보다).
Dohyun asks whether I watched the movie yesterday, but I couldn't.

fk: 친구가 이 가방이 비싸냐지만 나는 값을 몰라요.
fe: A friend asks if this bag is expensive, but I don't know the price.
xk: 형용사와 명사에 붙어서 '~냐고 묻지만 ~해요'라는 뜻이에요. 받침이 없으면 -냐지만, 받침이 있으면 -으냐지만을 써요. ㅂ불규칙 형용사는 '춥다 → 추우냐지만'처럼 써요. 명사는 N(이)냐지만을 써요.
xe: With adjectives and nouns, it means 'someone asks ~, but ~.' Use -냐지만 after a vowel and -으냐지만 after a final consonant. ㅂ-irregular adjectives change like 춥다 → 추우냐지만. Nouns take N(이)냐지만.
nk: 다른 사람이 상태를 묻는 말을 전하면서, 그 질문에 시원하게 대답하지 못할 때 써요. 뒤에는 모른다거나 아직 안 했다는 말이 자주 와요. 말할 때는 '-냐고 하지만'도 많이 써요.
ne: You use it to report someone's question about a state when you can't give a clear answer. The ending often says 'I don't know' or 'I haven't done it yet.' In speech, -냐고 하지만 is also common.
ex: 엄마가 방이 추우냐지만 나는 잘 몰라요.
Mom asks if the room is cold, but I don't really know.
손님이 이 커피가 뜨거우냐지만 나는 마셔 보지 않았어요.
A customer asks if this coffee is hot, but I haven't tried it.
아이가 저 사람이 의사냐지만 나는 이름도 몰라요.
The child asks if that person is a doctor, but I don't even know their name.
회사 후배가 이번 일이 어려우냐지만 나는 아직 시작하지 않았어요.
A junior colleague asks if this task is hard, but I haven't started yet.
cz: 서연이 이 옷이 ___ 나는 입어 보지 않았어요 (크다).
Seoyeon asks if this piece of clothing is big, but I haven't tried it on.
Mike asks if that building is a bank, but I don't know.

use: 어떤 일을 앞으로 계속 해 가다
fk: 우리는 어려운 문제를 하나씩 풀어 나가요.
fe: We are working through the hard problems one by one.
xk: 어떤 일을 앞으로 계속 해요. 동사 어간에 -아/어/여 나가다를 붙여요. 어간의 마지막 모음이 ㅏ, ㅗ이면 -아 나가다, 그 밖의 모음이면 -어 나가다, 하다는 해 나가다예요.
xe: It means to keep doing something and move forward with it. Add -아/어/여 나가다 to a verb stem: -아 when the last vowel of the stem is ㅏ or ㅗ, -어 for other vowels, and 하다 becomes 해 나가다.
nk: 시간이 걸리는 일을 조금씩 계속 해서 앞으로 나아가는 느낌이에요. 어려움을 이기거나 일을 하나씩 처리할 때 자주 써요. -고 있다는 지금 하고 있다는 뜻이고, -는 중이다는 지금 그 일을 하는 순간을 말해요. 나가다는 앞으로도 이어 간다는 느낌이 있어요.
ne: It gives a sense of steady progress on something that takes time. It is common for overcoming difficulties or handling tasks one by one. -고 있다 says it is happening now, and -는 중이다 points to the moment of doing it. 나가다 also suggests you will keep it going.
ex: 처음에는 힘들었지만 매일 연습해 나가면 늘어요.
It was hard at first, but if you keep practicing every day, you'll improve.
지민은 회사에서 새 프로젝트를 해 나가고 있어요.
Jimin is carrying out a new project at work.
Seoyeon got through her painful feelings.
가게 주인은 손님과 믿음을 조금씩 쌓아 나가고 있어요.
The shop owner is slowly building trust with customers.
마이크는 한국어 단어를 매일 열 개씩 외워 나갈 거예요.
Mike will keep memorizing ten Korean words every day.
cz: I will keep learning Korean songs from now on.
Hajun is correcting the mistakes one by one.

use: 같은 일을 자주 해서 습관이 몸에 배다
fe: If you get into the habit of going to bed late, mornings are hard.
xk: 같은 일을 자주 해서 습관이 몸에 뱄다는 뜻이에요. 동사 어간에 -아/어/여를 붙이고 '버릇하다'를 써요.
xe: It means you did something so often that it became a habit. Add -아/어/여 to the verb stem, then 버릇하다.
nk: 주로 고치기 힘든 나쁜 습관에 써요. '버릇하면', '버릇해서' 모양으로 많이 써요. '-곤 하다'는 그냥 자주 한다는 뜻이에요. '버릇하다'는 자꾸 해서 습관이 몸에 밴다는 점이 달라요. '-기 일쑤이다'는 안 좋은 일이 자주 생긴다는 뜻이에요.
ne: It is mostly used for habits that are hard to break, often in the forms 버릇하면 and 버릇해서. -곤 하다 just means 'do often'; 버릇하다 stresses that doing it again and again makes it a habit that sticks. -기 일쑤이다 means a bad thing happens all the time.
ex: 밥을 급히 먹어 버릇하면 배가 아파요.
If you get used to eating fast, your stomach hurts.
지민은 숙제를 미뤄 버릇해서 늘 바빠요.
Jimin has gotten into the habit of putting off homework, so Jimin is always busy.
사라는 밤마다 간식을 먹어 버릇해서 아침에 속이 안 좋아요.
Sara has gotten into the habit of eating snacks every night, so Sara's stomach feels bad in the morning.
하준은 약속에 늦어 버릇해서 친구들이 화를 내요.
Hajun has gotten into the habit of being late for appointments, so Hajun's friends get angry.
You shouldn't get into the habit of lying.
유나는 화가 나면 소리를 질러 버릇해서 친구들이 무서워해요.
Yuna has gotten into the habit of shouting when angry, so Yuna's friends are scared.
cz: 수진은 용돈을 막 ___ 늘 돈이 없어요. (쓰다 + -아/어 버릇하다 + -아서)
Sujin has gotten into the habit of spending her allowance carelessly, so she never has money.
에밀리는 누워서 TV를 ___ 목이 아파요. (보다 + -아/어 버릇하다 + -아서)
Emily has gotten into the habit of watching TV lying down, so Emily's neck hurts.

use: 다른 사람의 질문 + 그래서 내가 한 말·행동
fk: 민수가 어디 가냬서 같이 학교에 갔어요.
fe: Minsu asked where I was going, so we went to school together.
xk: 다른 사람이 물어서 그 때문에 내가 한 말이나 행동을 이어서 말해요. '-냐고 해서'의 줄임말이에요. 동사는 -(느)냬서, 형용사는 -(으)냬서, 명사는 (이)냬서를 써요. 과거는 -았/었냬서(먹었냬서)예요.
xe: You report a question someone asked, then say what you said or did because of it. It is the short form of -냐고 해서. Use -(느)냬서 for verbs, -(으)냬서 for adjectives, and (이)냬서 for nouns. The past is -았/었냬서, as in 먹었냬서.
nk: 말할 때 쓰는 줄임 표현이에요. 글에서는 '-냐고 해서'를 써요. 뒤에는 그 질문 때문에 내가 한 대답이나 행동이 와요.
ne: It is a spoken contraction. In writing, use -냐고 해서. What follows is your answer or action prompted by the question.
ex: 엄마가 뭐 먹느냬서 김밥을 먹는다고 했어요.
Mom asked what I was eating, so I said I was eating kimbap.
친구가 요즘 바쁘냬서 별로 안 바쁘다고 했어요.
A friend asked if I was busy lately, so I said I wasn't very busy.
선생님이 숙제가 많으냬서 아주 많다고 했어요.
The teacher asked if there was a lot of homework, so I said there was a lot.
하준이 이게 얼마냬서 만 원이라고 했어요.
Hajun asked how much this was, so I said it was ten thousand won.
사라가 어제 뭐 했냬서 영화를 봤다고 했어요.
Sara asked what I did yesterday, so I said I watched a movie.
직원이 봉투가 필요하냬서 필요 없다고 했어요.
The clerk asked if I needed a bag, so I said I didn't.
cz: 지우가 점심을 ___ 아직 안 먹었다고 했어요. (먹다)
Jiu asked if I had eaten lunch, so I said I hadn't eaten yet.
Seoyeon asked if the room was big, so I said it was very small.

use: 다른 사람의 질문 + 그 사람의 다음 행동
fk: 수진이 어디 가냐더니 먼저 가 버렸어요.
fe: Sujin asked where I was going, and then she left first.
xk: 남이 물어본 말을 전하고, 그 사람이 그다음에 한 일을 말해요. '-냐고 하더니'의 줄임말이에요. 동사는 -(느)냐더니, 형용사는 -(으)냐더니, 과거는 -았/었냐더니예요.
xe: You report a question someone asked, then say what that same person did next. It is the short form of -냐고 하더니. Use -(느)냐더니 for verbs, -(으)냐더니 for adjectives, and (이)냐더니 for nouns. The past is -았/었냐더니, as in 먹었냐더니. The subject is usually the same in both clauses.
nk: 질문한 사람이 그다음에 한 행동을 내가 보고 말해요. 질문과 이어지는 행동이 오거나, 뜻밖의 행동이 와요. 질문을 듣고 내가 한 일을 말할 때는 '-냬서'를 써요.
ne: You describe what the asker did next, as something you saw yourself. What follows is an action connected to the question, or a surprising one. To say what you did after hearing a question, use -냬서 instead.
ex: Mom asked if I was hungry, then cooked me ramen.
친구가 한국어가 어려우냐더니 책을 빌려 줬어요.
A friend asked if Korean was hard, then lent me a book.
서연이 저 건물이 뭐냐더니 사진을 찍었어요.
Seoyeon asked what that building was, then took a photo of it.
가게 주인이 이게 마음에 드느냐더니 값을 올렸어요.
The shop owner asked if I liked it, then raised the price.
The teacher asked if I had done my homework, then checked it right away.
cz: Dohyeon asked if I had eaten dinner, then cooked ramen for me.
Yuna asked if the room was hot, then opened the window.

f: V 어간·있다/없다·-았/었-+나 싶다 · A-(으)ㄴ가 싶다 · N인가 싶다
fe: It was dark outside, so I wondered if it was raining.
xk: 확실하지 않지만 '혹시 그런가?' 하고 생각할 때 써요. 동사, 있다/없다, 지난 일(-았/었-) 뒤에는 -나 싶다를 쓰고, 형용사는 -(으)ㄴ가 싶다, 명사는 N인가 싶다를 써요.
xe: Use it when you are not sure but wonder whether something is so. After verbs, 있다/없다 and past -았/었-, use -나 싶다; adjectives take -(으)ㄴ가 싶다 and nouns take N인가 싶다.
nk: 마음속으로 조심스럽게 짐작하거나 걱정하는 느낌이에요. '제가 너무 심했나 싶어요'처럼 자기가 한 일을 돌아볼 때 많이 쓰고, '-나 싶어서'로 이어 그 생각 때문에 한 일을 말하기도 해요. '-지 않을까 싶다'는 자기 의견을 부드럽게 내놓는 말이고, '-나 싶다'는 혹시 그런지 걱정하거나 의심하는 마음에 더 가까워요.
ne: It sounds like a cautious guess or worry in your own mind. It is common when looking back on something you did (제가 너무 심했나 싶어요), and -나 싶어서 explains what you did because of that thought. -지 않을까 싶다 gently offers your opinion, while -나 싶다 is closer to worrying or doubting whether something is so.
ex: 친구가 답장을 안 해서 화가 났나 싶어요.
My friend isn't replying, so I wonder if she's angry.
문밖에서 소리가 나서 누가 왔나 싶었어요.
I heard a sound outside the door, so I wondered if someone had come.
어제 제가 말을 너무 심하게 했나 싶어요.
I wonder if I spoke too harshly yesterday.
I took a taxi because I thought I might be late.
이 옷이 좀 작은가 싶어서 큰 걸로 바꿨어요.
I thought this top might be a bit small, so I exchanged it for a bigger one.
cz: 가게 불이 꺼져 있어서 벌써 문을 ___ 싶어서 걱정했어요. (닫다, 지난 일)
The store lights were off, so I was worried it had already closed.
메시지를 보냈는데 답이 없어요. 제가 뭘 ___ 싶어요. (잘못하다, 지난 일)
I sent a message but there's no reply. I wonder if I did something wrong.

fe: I'm thinking about getting my hair cut short.
xk: 아직 정하지 않았고, 할지 말지 지금 생각하고 있는 일을 말할 때 써요. 동사 어간에 -(으)ㄹ까를 붙이고 뒤에 '생각 중이에요'를 써요. 받침이 있으면 -을까, 없으면 -ㄹ까예요. ㄹ 받침 동사는 그대로 '까'만 붙여요(만들다 → 만들까).
xe: Use it for something you have not decided yet and are still thinking over. Add -(으)ㄹ까 to a verb stem, then say 생각 중이에요. Use -을까 after a final consonant and -ㄹ까 after a vowel. Stems that end in ㄹ just add 까 (만들다 → 만들까).
nk: '-(으)ㄹ까 해요'와 뜻이 거의 같아요. '생각 중'이라는 말이 있어서 지금 고민하고 있다는 느낌이 더 분명해요. 이미 정한 일에는 '-기로 했어요'나 '-(으)ㄹ 거예요'를 써요. 자기 계획을 말할 때 쓰고, 형용사에는 쓰지 않아요. '살까 말까 생각 중이에요'처럼 '말까'를 넣으면 할지 말지 망설이는 마음이 더 잘 보여요. '뭘 먹을까 생각 중이에요'처럼 뭐·어디·언제와 같이 쓰면 무엇을 고를지 고민한다는 뜻이에요.
ne: It means almost the same as -(으)ㄹ까 해요. The words 생각 중 make it clearer that you are thinking it over right now. For something already decided, use -기로 했어요 or -(으)ㄹ 거예요. Use it for your own plans, and not with adjectives. Adding 말까 (살까 말까 생각 중이에요) shows more clearly that you cannot decide whether to do it or not. With a question word such as 뭐, 어디 or 언제 (뭘 먹을까 생각 중이에요), it means you are wondering which one to choose.
ex: 이번 휴가에 바다에 갈까 생각 중이에요.
I'm thinking about going to the sea for this vacation.
내년에 한국어 시험을 볼까 생각 중이에요.
I'm thinking about taking a Korean test next year.
강아지를 한 마리 키울까 생각 중이에요.
I'm thinking about getting a puppy.
차를 살까 말까 아직 생각 중이에요.
I'm still thinking about whether or not to buy a car.
I was thinking about what to eat for dinner.
cz: I'm thinking about learning to swim. It's good for my health.
I'm thinking about reading a book at home this weekend.
